summary: BIER forwards multicast without per-flow state in the core. The ingress router decides which egress routers need a packet and puts that information in a header. This document defines the BIER encapsulation for MPLS and non-MPLS networks.

eli5.summary: This defines the exact layout of the label on the envelope that lists who should get a copy.

subtitle: The exact header that lets a multicast packet carry a bit for every router that should receive it.

tldr.problem: BIER forwards multicast without per-flow state, but routers need to agree on one header format that carries the set of egress routers, in both MPLS and non-MPLS networks.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress router wraps each packet in a BIER header whose BitString has one bit per egress router. In MPLS the first four octets double as the bottom MPLS label stack entry; in non-MPLS networks a domain-wide BIFT-id takes the label's place.
tldr.outcome: The encapsulation lets every router read the BitString, find the right forwarding table and replicate the packet as needed. It has no cryptographic protection, so BIER packets should not be accepted from untrusted interfaces.

today: The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 8296. It is the reference for the BIER header, and RFC 8279 describes the architecture it supports.

sections.title: What the BIER Encapsulation Does
sections.content:
Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) is the multicast architecture described in RFC 8279. It delivers multicast packets through a BIER domain without tree-building protocols and without per-flow state in intermediate routers. This RFC defines the header that makes that possible.

A packet enters the domain at a Bit-Forwarding Ingress Router (BFIR) and leaves at one or more Bit-Forwarding Egress Routers (BFERs). Each router in a domain has a BFR-id, a number in the range 1 to 65535 that is unique within a sub-domain (SD). The header carries the information needed to forward the packet: a BitString, plus values that identify the sub-domain, the Set Identifier (SI) and the BitString length (BSL).

The same header works in MPLS networks and, with small differences, in non-MPLS networks. The payload after the header can be an IPv4 packet, an IPv6 packet, an Ethernet frame, an MPLS packet or an OAM packet.
sections.eli5: BIER puts a row of tick boxes on each packet, one box per receiver. This document says exactly how that row of boxes is laid out on the packet.

sections.title: The BIER Header Layout
sections.content:
The header starts with a BIFT-id, which names a particular Bit Index Forwarding Table (BIFT). Each BIFT matches one combination of sub-domain, BSL and SI, so the packet does not need to carry those three values explicitly. A router finds the BitString length from the BIFT-id.

The first four octets hold the BIFT-id, a Traffic Class (TC), the S bit and a TTL. The next four octets hold Nibble, Ver, BSL and a 20-bit Entropy field. The third group holds OAM, Rsv, DSCP, Proto and the 16-bit BFIR-id. The BitString follows.

The default BitString length for these encapsulations is 256.
sections.eli5: The top of the packet is a label with a few small fields: which table to use, how many hops are left, and what is inside. After that comes the long row of tick boxes.

sections.title: Using BIER in MPLS Networks
sections.content:
In an MPLS network the BIFT-id is an MPLS label, called a BIER-MPLS label. Each router advertises one label per combination of sub-domain, SI and BSL it uses, through IGP extensions (or BGP extensions where BGP is the only routing protocol). The labels are locally significant, downstream-assigned labels, and penultimate hop popping MUST NOT be applied to them.

For example, with one sub-domain, a BSL of 256 and BFR-ids up to 512, two SIs are needed (SI=0 and SI=1), so each router advertises two labels. Labels only need to be assigned if they will be used.

The first four octets of the BIER header are also the last four octets of the MPLS label stack, so the S bit MUST be 1 there and any earlier label stack entries MUST have S clear. The label stack entry's TC keeps its usual MPLS meaning.

After the label stack, the Nibble field is set to binary 0101, so MPLS equal-cost multipath logic will not mistake the rest of the header for an IP header or a pseudowire packet. A router that sees any other value SHOULD discard the packet and log an error.
sections.eli5: On an MPLS network the first label doubles as the table name. Each neighbor tells you which label means which table, and you swap in the neighbor's label every time you pass the packet on.

sections.title: Fields, TTL and Next Protocol
sections.content:
Ver is the header version; this document defines version 0, and a router that does not support the version MUST discard the packet and log an error. The 4-bit BSL field encodes the BitString length as log2(k)-5 and is there for offline tools. A router MUST infer the length from the BIFT-id and MUST NOT use this field. The permitted values are 1 to 7, meaning 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048 and 4096 bits.

Entropy is a 20-bit value for load balancing: two packets with the same entropy and the same BitString MUST take the same path. Proto is a 6-bit Next Protocol value from an IANA registry that says what the payload is. BFIR-id is by default the BFR-id of the ingress router.

The TTL must be one less on a forwarded packet than the incoming TTL. If the incoming TTL is 1 or greater and a bit in the BitString identifies the current router, that router acts as a BFER and processes the payload. A packet with an incoming TTL of 0, or of 1 with a set bit for some other router, is expired and SHOULD go to an error-handling procedure. A packet with TTL 1 that is delivered to this router MUST NOT be forwarded further.

The two OAM bits default to 0 and do not change path or quality of service. The two Rsv bits SHOULD be 0 on transmission and MUST be ignored on reception. By default DSCP is not used in MPLS networks, and its six bits SHOULD be 0.
sections.eli5: Each packet has a countdown so it cannot wander forever, a note saying what is inside, and a number that keeps packets of the same conversation on the same road.

sections.title: Non-MPLS Networks and Outer Encapsulation
sections.content:
Without MPLS, a BIFT-id MUST be assigned for every combination of sub-domain, SI and BSL in use. The mapping is the same across the whole domain and does not change from router to router. How BIFT-ids are assigned and distributed is outside the scope of this document.

Several fields change. TC has no default meaning: it SHOULD be 000 on transmission and MUST be ignored. The S bit SHOULD be 1 on transmission and MUST be ignored. Nibble SHOULD be 0000 and MUST be ignored. DSCP MAY carry a Differentiated Services Codepoint, but its meaning is out of scope.

A BIER packet may be carried inside another frame or packet, which is assumed to be unicast between neighboring routers. In MPLS, the outer next-protocol codepoint for MPLS MUST be used; for Ethernet that is Ethertype 0x8847. For non-MPLS BIER, the codepoint MUST mean non-MPLS BIER and MUST NOT mean MPLS, so the Ethertype MUST NOT be 0x8847 or 0x8848. IEEE has assigned Ethertype 0xAB37 for non-MPLS BIER.
sections.eli5: Outside MPLS, the table names are the same everywhere, so no swapping is needed. A special envelope marking tells the next router that this is BIER and not ordinary MPLS mail.

sections.title: Imposing and Processing the Header
sections.content:
The BFIR knows the MTU of the BIER domain and the size of the encapsulation, so it can work out the largest payload, called the BIER-MTU. If a packet is too large, the BFIR does whatever is normal for an oversized multicast packet: drop it and advertise the BIER-MTU, or fragment it.

To encapsulate a packet, the BFIR determines the Proto value and the set of BFERs from the multicast flow overlay. It assigns the packet to a sub-domain if more than one is supported, looks up each BFER's BFR-id, and converts the ids into SI and BitString form. For each distinct SI it makes a copy with a BitString for the destinations in that SI, then applies the forwarding procedure of RFC 8279.

In MPLS, the BFIR finds the BIER-MPLS label advertised by the neighbor for that sub-domain, SI and BSL, and pushes it with the S bit set. An intermediate router that sees one of its own BIER-MPLS labels infers the BSL, SI and sub-domain from it, forwards per RFC 8279 and swaps the label for the one the neighbor advertised, with TTL one less. In non-MPLS networks the router infers the same values from the BIFT-id.

If the payload is an MPLS packet, an MPLS label stack follows the BIER header, separate from any stack before it.
sections.eli5: The first router decides who gets a copy and ticks the boxes. If the receivers do not fit in one row of boxes, it sends one packet for each row. Every router after that just reads the ticks and passes copies along.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The encapsulation inherits the security considerations of the MPLS data plane, of the IGP extensions it relies on, and of RFC 8279. It offers no cryptographic integrity protection, so changes to the header that are not part of normal forwarding may go undetected and packets may be lost, stolen or misdelivered.

Layer 2 encryption can protect packets between adjacent routers, but nothing can stop a compromised router from altering the header or misforwarding. BIER-encapsulated packets should generally not be accepted from untrusted interfaces or tunnels. The header itself cannot prove that a source is legitimate, that it really is the system named in BFIR-id, or that it may set particular bits in the BitString.
sections.eli5: The row of ticks is not locked. Anyone who can change it could send mail to the wrong people, so only accept these packets from routers you trust.
